I've been following the Credit NFT collection launch by @jackbutcher via @XMoney and am quite intrigued. The art is cool, the X money transaction mechanism is novel and the mechanics are interestingly designed.

There's an interesting supply/demand dynamic to them also. After launching a few nights ago, there are ~122,000 Credit NFTs in circulation. In ~1 week, you can burn 80 Credits to make a Statement NFT, equating to 1,526 total possible Statements (~122,000/80).

If launched today, ~392 Statements would be able to be minted across ~241 holders (~26% of the total available Statements). For the full 1,526 to be able to be minted, ~37,000 Credits would need to be acquired by other wallets with less than 80. There are ~9,000 Credits listed on @opensea right now. More can be listed at any time and there's nothing that says all Statements need to be minted, but it will be interesting to see how this experiment plays out.

@Pumpfun products generated $38.28M in fees over seven days on @DefiLlama.

That's more than @Uniswap $35.92M, which honestly surprised me.

The reason is simple: Pump can charge up to 1.25% per trade, while most Uniswap pools charge 0.01%–0.30%.

Memecoin traders also buy and sell constantly, so the same money generates fees again and again across launches, bonding curves, and PumpSwap.

I wonder whether this is another memecoin phase that eventually dies down, or something Pump can actually sustain.

#Uranium #Silver #Copper #Gold

⚡ DAILY METALS PULSE | 24 September 2026

US jobless claims fell to 197,000, below expectations, while renewed Middle East supply fears pushed oil higher. That keeps inflation and further Fed tightening firmly in focus.

Higher borrowing costs are squeezing metals today—and could make tomorrow’s supply more expensive to build.

☢️ URANIUM
The latest NEA/IAEA report says identified resources can meet projected demand through 2050. The challenge is turning them into production: new uranium mines typically take 15–20 years to develop. Financing, permits and long-term contracts remain essential.

🥈 SILVER
The 2026 forecast already allows for a 7% increase in recycling and still projects a 46.3-million-ounce deficit. Extra scrap helps, but the market remains undersupplied even with softer industrial demand.

🔶 COPPER
Capstone’s planned sale of Cozamin to Luca Mining for up to US$385 million would release capital for its growth pipeline. A useful reminder that expanding copper supply requires substantial funding—and successful project delivery.

🥇 GOLD
Global gold ETFs attracted US$18 billion in August, their second-largest monthly inflow on record. September’s pressure from rates and the dollar is testing that appetite. I’m watching whether investment demand holds through the latest rise in yields.

Funding, construction and physical flows deserve just as much attention as the next Fed headline.

Steve Hilton: “California has become a state where if you do the right thing, you're punished, and if you do the wrong thing, you're rewarded. That is upside down, but that's the story beneath everything, and that's what we need to turn around. That's what this election is actually about.”

“There's this Latino couple who wanted me to come and see their business in South Central LA. It's not Skid Row, but it's pretty rough, and it's the usual squalor that I'm afraid we're used to in this city because they don't know how to run the place.

But in the middle of all that squalor, this beautiful little store. It's a shoe store, and they've been running it fourteen years. Latino couple.

We went in, we were talking, they gave me all the usual things that I'm very familiar with; the taxes, the ridiculous bureaucracy, the permits that get more complicated and costly every year, the electric bill, et cetera.

They said, ‘But that's not why we wanted you to come here. Come with me.’ They took me outside.

We went for a walk, two city blocks. Could have gone even further. Every single part of the sidewalk: street vendors.

You think, ‘Illegal street vendors. What are they selling?’ Shoes and apparel and T-shirts. Just the entire sidewalk.

This 14-year business, a lovely little local business, everything spotless, everything clean, exactly what we would want to see, is going out of business because you've got people there that are not paying taxes, not paying electric, not paying rent, not complying with any licensing.

And then I said to the guy, ‘When did all this happen? Has this been here all the time you've been here?’

‘No, it's the last six or seven years.’

I said, ‘Is it something to do with the pandemic?’

‘No.’

I looked into it. Eight years ago, in 2018, they passed a bill in Sacramento to legalize street vending in California across the state. Cities can't do anything about it. Counties can't do anything about it.

What does it tell you when you take that into account?”

@SteveHiltonx

Look what I dug up... the GMI Monthly from May 2014.

We'd just held the first ever GMI Round Table, and a couple of members who'd backed a Bitcoin exchange in Singapore got up to talk. I was expecting something about payments. Instead they completely blew my mind. I went back to my desk and wrote that if you could record anything on an onchain ledger you'd have proof of ownership of everything... every insurance contract, every housing deal, every stock and bond...

At the time that sounded ludicrous. Putting a stock on a blockchain felt like science fiction. 

What I understand now is this is far far far bigger than that. Agents are about to become the most active participants in the economy, and the only thing they can read, verify and trade is a token. So everything they need has to become one... money, identity, permissions, data, compute, political opinions, beliefs, information itself...

Literally everything will be a token.

tweets.text:
Friends, work is getting so hilarious right now!

My agents run in a loop with /goal. When they need context, they DM one of my colleagues on Teams. But some of my colleagues are also using agents, so their agent replies to mine.

My agent is basically asking another person’s agent for context that is not in either person’s brain. It’s somewhere in their emails, documents, meetings, or cloud storage. The other agent finds it, sends it back, and mine keeps working toward my goal.

It feels obvious that agent-to-agent communication is about to become insanely fast. Most of it is just context exchange.

The next step is a company brain where all the context lives, with access rights attached. Instead of messaging five people, your agent retrieves exactly what it is allowed to know and continues working.

The funniest part: I was grabbing a coffee when a colleague received a Teams message “from me.” He looked at me, saw that I was obviously not typing, and immediately understood that it was my agent.

We are already becoming managers of agents talking to other agents.

I asked it about its memory pipeline, its scheduler, its token usage, and it walked me through everything: the nightly dream files, the feed jobs, the heartbeat cron, the exact prompt it uses to generate my feed etc etc. You can inspect the Muse DB and basically everything. 

It feels like you own the thing.

You may have noticed that over the past month, most agents and AI apps have started proactively setting reminders, scheduling background tasks, and checking back later. Basically cron jobs at scale.

I think we’ll see a lot more of this for two reasons:

1/Many tasks outlast a chat. If I’m trying to get a restaurant reservation, the agent should check every hour for an opening and tell me when it finds one. If you work on an Excel it could say "I will update this workbook once MSFT reports earnings next."

2/ AI has a retention problem. People forget to open the app. But if an agent comes back with an update on something you actually care about, you have a reason to return.

Giving an agent this ability is conceptually simple: give it a scheduling tool and tell it in the system prompt that it can use it. The hard part is reliably running billions of scheduled jobs at scale.
